questions.stem: Classify this sentence by structure: "The head girl and the senior prefect addressed the assembly on Monday morning."
questions.explanation: Structure is decided by counting clauses, not words. There is only one finite verb here, *addressed*, so there is only one clause and the sentence is simple. A compound subject joined by *and* does not create a second clause because the two nouns share the same verb.

distractorRationale.b: Students see *and* and assume compound, but *and* only joins two subjects here, not two clauses
distractorRationale.c: A complex sentence needs at least one subordinate clause, and there is none
distractorRationale.d: This would need both a second main clause and a subordinate clause

questions.stem: Classify this sentence by structure: "The rain fell heavily, but the match continued."
questions.explanation: There are two finite verbs, *fell* and *continued*, and each clause could stand alone as a sentence. They are joined by the coordinating conjunction *but*, so the two clauses are of equal rank and the sentence is compound.

distractorRationale.a: A simple sentence has only one clause, but this one has two
distractorRationale.c: A complex sentence needs a subordinate clause; both clauses here are independent
distractorRationale.d: There is no subordinate clause to add to the two main clauses

questions.stem: Classify this sentence by structure: "Although the school fees were increased, enrolment rose sharply."
questions.explanation: A complex sentence has one main clause and at least one subordinate clause. Here *enrolment rose sharply* is the main clause, while *Although the school fees were increased* is subordinate because *Although* prevents it from standing alone.

distractorRationale.a: There are two finite verbs, *were increased* and *rose*, so there are two clauses
distractorRationale.b: A compound sentence needs two clauses that could each stand alone; the first cannot
distractorRationale.d: This pattern would require two main clauses as well as the subordinate clause

questions.stem: Classify this sentence by structure: "When the results were released, the students celebrated and their parents gave thanks."
questions.explanation: Count the clauses: *When the results were released* is subordinate, while *the students celebrated* and *their parents gave thanks* are two main clauses joined by *and*. Two main clauses plus at least one subordinate clause makes the sentence compound-complex.

distractorRationale.a: There are three finite verbs, so there are three clauses
distractorRationale.b: Compound covers only the two main clauses and ignores the subordinate *When* clause
distractorRationale.c: Complex would be right if there were only one main clause, but there are two

questions.stem: Classify this sentence by function: "Submit your continuous assessment scores before Friday."
questions.explanation: An imperative sentence gives a command, an instruction or a request. Its subject *you* is understood rather than written, which is why the sentence appears to begin with the verb *Submit*.

distractorRationale.a: A declarative sentence states a fact and has a stated subject
distractorRationale.b: An interrogative sentence asks a question and ends with a question mark
distractorRationale.d: An exclamatory sentence expresses strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is exclamatory?

options.text: How did she finish the paper so quickly?
How quickly she finished the paper!

questions.explanation: An exclamatory sentence expresses strong feeling and typically begins with *How* or *What* in statement word order, ending with an exclamation mark. Notice that option b keeps the subject before the verb — *she finished* — whereas the question in option a inverts them to *did she finish*.

distractorRationale.a: Begins with *How* but inverts subject and auxiliary and ends with a question mark, so it is interrogative
distractorRationale.c: States a fact in neutral word order, so it is declarative
distractorRationale.d: Gives a command with an understood subject, so it is imperative

questions.stem: "Because the generator had broken down again." What is wrong with this group of words, and how is it best corrected?

options.text: Nothing is wrong; it is a complete simple sentence.
It is a fragment; attach it to a main clause, as in "The hall was dark because the generator had broken down again."
It is a run-on sentence; separate it with a semicolon.
It is a comma splice; replace the full stop with a comma.

questions.explanation: The group has a subject and a finite verb but begins with the subordinator *Because*, so it is a subordinate clause punctuated as though it were a sentence — a fragment. The repair is to supply the main clause it depends on, or to delete the subordinator.

distractorRationale.a: A subordinate clause standing alone cannot be a complete sentence
distractorRationale.c: A run-on has too many clauses joined wrongly; this has too few
distractorRationale.d: A comma splice occurs when two main clauses are joined by a comma, which is not the situation here

questions.stem: Which option corrects the comma splice in "The bus was full, we waited for the next one"?

options.text: The bus was full we waited for the next one.
The bus was full, so we waited for the next one.
The bus was full, however we waited for the next one.
The bus was full, therefore, we waited for the next one.

questions.explanation: A comma alone cannot join two main clauses. The cleanest repairs are to add a coordinating conjunction after the comma, to use a semicolon, or to write two separate sentences. Adding *so* gives a correct compound sentence and also expresses the cause-and-effect link.

distractorRationale.a: Removing the comma creates a run-on sentence, which is worse
distractorRationale.c: *However* is a conjunctive adverb and needs a semicolon or full stop before it, not a comma
distractorRationale.d: *Therefore* has the same problem as *however*, and it also contradicts nothing

questions.stem: A simple sentence must always be short.
questions.explanation: False. A simple sentence is defined by having exactly one clause, not by its length. "After a long and exhausting journey through the flooded roads of the delta, the weary relief workers finally reached the camp" contains one finite verb, *reached*, so it is a simple sentence despite being over twenty words long.

questions.stem: How many clauses are there in the sentence "The nurse who treated my brother said that the swelling would subside if he rested"?
questions.explanation: Count the finite verbs: *treated*, *said*, *would subside* and *rested* — four verbs, so four clauses. They are the main clause *The nurse ... said ...*, the adjectival clause *who treated my brother*, the noun clause *that the swelling would subside*, and the adverbial clause of condition *if he rested*.

distractorRationale.a: Counts only the two most obvious clauses and misses the embedded ones
distractorRationale.b: Usually results from overlooking the *if* clause
distractorRationale.d: Counts *would subside* as two clauses; an auxiliary plus main verb is a single verb phrase

questions.stem: Classify this sentence by structure: "I enjoy reading novels and writing poetry."
questions.explanation: The sentence contains two independent clauses joined by the conjunction 'and', making it a compound sentence. Each clause can stand alone as a complete sentence.

distractorRationale.a: A simple sentence has only one independent clause.
distractorRationale.c: A complex sentence contains an independent clause and at least one dependent clause.
distractorRationale.d: A compound-complex sentence contains at least two independent clauses and one or more dependent clauses.

questions.stem: Which option corrects the run-on sentence: "I love to read I go to the library every week."?

options.text: I love to read; I go to the library every week.
I love to read and I go to the library every week.
I love to read, I go to the library every week.
I love to read. I go to the library every week.

questions.explanation: The correct way to fix a run-on sentence is to use a semicolon or a period to separate the independent clauses. Both options 'a' and 'd' are correct, but 'a' is the best choice for maintaining a close relationship between the clauses.

distractorRationale.b: Using 'and' creates a compound sentence but does not correct the run-on.
distractorRationale.c: This is a comma splice, which is also incorrect.
